source: Friston, FitzGerald, Rigoli, Schwartenbeck, Pezzulo (2017) Active inference: a process theory
finding: Expected free energy G of a policy splits into extrinsic value (log evidence of preferred outcomes) and epistemic value (expected information gain, the mutual information between hidden states and outcomes). Epistemic value is how the theory defines curiosity.
numbers: G = -(mutual information between states and outcomes) - E[ln P(outcome)]; equivalently expected cost (KL of predicted vs preferred outcomes) plus expected ambiguity.
quote: epistemic value can be thought of as driving curiosity and novelty-seeking behavior
limits: All of this is under the agent's own generative model. Preferences are priors, so the split depends on how they are set.
agent_relevance: Gives a computable score for which probe resolves most uncertainty. Our S7 select and S3 open mode can use expected information gain over a hypothesis set.

source: Friston, FitzGerald, Rigoli, Schwartenbeck, Pezzulo (2017) Active inference: a process theory
finding: The explore-to-exploit switch is automatic. Information gain is a KL divergence and cannot be below zero. When the posterior is no longer informed by new observations, epistemic value is the same for all policies and preferences decide.
numbers: Epistemic value never exceeds zero; best case is zero when a preferred outcome has probability 1.
quote: when there is no posterior uncertainty ... epistemic value will be the same for all policies, allowing preferences to dictate action
limits: Switch is exact only if the model is right. A mis-specified model can feel certain and stop exploring too early.
agent_relevance: Maps to a stop rule for open mode: leave S3 when the best probe's expected information gain is about zero, not on a clock (fits G1).

source: Friston, FitzGerald, Rigoli, Schwartenbeck, Pezzulo (2017) Active inference: a process theory
finding: T-maze simulation: the agent first visits the cue arm (epistemic policy), then the reward arm. After enough trials with a fixed context it goes straight to reward.
numbers: 32 trials, 10 policies. First ~20 trials epistemic (cue then reward). After that direct reward. Reaction time drops and mean utility rises. Policies with relative posterior below 1/128 were dropped.
limits: Simulation only, one toy task, hand-set preferences. One null outcome on trial 12 briefly raised policy uncertainty.
agent_relevance: Shows the switch point depends on learned confidence about context. Cheap probes first, then commit.

source: Friston, FitzGerald, Rigoli, Schwartenbeck, Pezzulo (2017) Active inference: a process theory
finding: With all outcomes given equal utility (no preferences), behaviour is still purposeful: the agent resolves context uncertainty at the cue and avoids mildly ambiguous arms. The balance between exploring and exploiting rests on the precision of prior preferences.
numbers: Figure 10: 32 trials; precision of preferences set to zero gives pure epistemic foraging.
quote: epistemic value can, on its own, specify behavior even if there are no explicit or extrinsic goals
limits: Exploration is limited to outcomes the model already entertains.
agent_relevance: A vague goal makes the agent explore more; a sharp goal makes it exploit. A knob for open versus focused mode.

source: Friston, FitzGerald, Rigoli, Schwartenbeck, Pezzulo (2017) Active inference: a process theory
finding: The process theory links to physiology: simulated repetition suppression, phasic dopamine as confidence in policy, and place-cell firing in epistemic foraging. These are model outputs, not new data.
numbers: Simulations over 32 trials; oddball minus standard difference waveform.
limits: Resemblance to ERP and dopamine data is qualitative, no fit statistics.
agent_relevance: Low direct use. Warns that neural support here is by resemblance.

source: Friston, Rigoli, Ognibene, Mathys, Fitzgerald, Pezzulo (2015) Active inference and epistemic value
finding: Founding paper for epistemic value in active inference (T-maze, expected free energy with salience). Not opened: paywalled, no open copy found. Known only through how opened papers describe it.
limits: Treat all specific claims as unconfirmed here; the 2017 process theory (a01-a05) restates the same T-maze result.
agent_relevance: Cite the opened 2017 paper as the working source.

source: Friston, FitzGerald, Rigoli, Schwartenbeck, Pezzulo (2017) Active inference: curiosity and insight
finding: Extends the scheme to structure learning and insight as Bayesian model reduction. Cited by the opened Da Costa 2020 review as the curiosity and abstract rule learning demo. Not opened.
limits: Title and role taken from citation context only.
agent_relevance: Possible link to the insight subfield (A12). Check before use.

source: Schwartenbeck, FitzGerald, Dolan, Friston (2013) Exploration, novelty, surprise, and free energy minimization
finding: Early argument that free-energy minimisation does not preclude exploration (the dark-room worry). Minimising surprise over future outcomes means matching likely to desired outcomes while keeping entropy over visited states, so new states raise the value of the current one.
quote: minimizing surprise leads naturally to concepts such as exploration and novelty bonuses
limits: Theory paper, no data. The authors say empirical and simulation papers will follow.
agent_relevance: Counters the worry that a minimise-error agent never explores; open mode can be built into the objective.

source: Parr & Friston (2017) Uncertainty, epistemics and active inference
finding: Epistemic foraging depends on the agent's beliefs about sensory precision and volatility. Salience falls where precision is low, and the salience of an unchanged location grows slowly as uncertainty about it grows. This gives inhibition of return and removes the dark-room problem.
numbers: In simulated visual search, saccades went less often to low-precision regions; higher believed volatility gave a shorter inhibition of return (fewer saccades between fixations).
quote: greater volatility led to a shorter inhibition of return
limits: Simulation; the mapping to acetylcholine (precision) and noradrenaline (volatility) is by analogy, citing outside data.
agent_relevance: Information value is not high entropy. A noisy source is not worth probing. Probe where uncertainty is resolvable.

source: Schwartenbeck, FitzGerald, Mathys, Dolan, Kronbichler, Friston (2019) Computational mechanisms of curiosity and goal-directed exploration
finding: Splits information gain in two. Hidden-state exploration (active inference) seeks unambiguous observations to infer the current state. Model-parameter exploration (active learning) seeks outcomes that teach the task structure. They can conflict.
numbers: Mutual information terms: parameter beliefs before vs after an observation (novelty); states (salience). Simulated risky-vs-safe choice: curious early picks, confident after about ten trials.
quote: an option will be very interesting ... if its outcomes are ambiguous due to high uncertainty about the mapping
limits: Simulations only in the opened text; behavioural predictions are for future human tests. Active learning needs context to be stable across trials.
agent_relevance: Two probe types for S3: which hypothesis is true now, versus what are the rules of this task. Different operators.

source: Schwartenbeck et al. (2019) eLife
finding: Prediction: uncertainty about parameters modulates the effect of state uncertainty. An ambiguous option is attractive while the agent is unsure what it maps to, and aversive once it is sure it is ambiguous. Mutual information is zero when the posterior stops changing, so active learning dies out.
limits: Untested in the opened text. Random exploration (Wilson 2014, Gershman 2018) is named as a separate human mechanism, not read.
agent_relevance: Track unsure and confidently-noisy separately before choosing a probe.

source: Sajid, Ball, Parr, Friston (2021) Active inference: demystified and compared
finding: Compares active inference to Bayesian RL and Q-learning on FrozenLake. With no reward, belief-based agents keep exploring; Q-learning does not. With a goal-only reward, all solve it. Active inference and Bayesian RL behave nearly the same once preferences are written as reward.
numbers: With no preferences, belief-based agents' average score stayed near 40-45 (exploring); Q-learning looped deterministically. With Dirichlet-learned preferences, after 5 trials the agent goes straight to the hole it prefers.
quote: exploration and exploitation as two different ways of tackling the same problem: minimizing uncertainty
limits: FrozenLake is small and discrete; authors say it is not representative. With the epistemic term removed, plain expected reward remains.
agent_relevance: Curiosity is cheap to add and fades by itself once learning is done. RL is the special case with no epistemic term.

source: Sajid et al. (2021) Active inference: demystified and compared
finding: The authors reject Millidge's variant that subtracts ambiguity, because it would make agents less ambiguity-averse and stop information seeking. They keep ambiguity in G.
limits: Design choice, not a test.
agent_relevance: The formula chosen decides whether the agent is curious. Pin it down in our spec.

source: Millidge, Tschantz, Buckley (2021) Whence the expected free energy?
finding: Epistemic value does not fall out of extending variational free energy into the future. The future free energy (FEF) has the opposite sign on information gain, so it discourages exploration. The EFE is the FEF minus expected information gain.
numbers: In FEF the epistemic term is positive (penalised); in EFE it is negative (rewarded).
quote: the FEF penalizes epistemic behavior whereas the EFE promotes it
limits: Pure derivation; the origin of the epistemic term is therefore a design choice, not a theorem.
agent_relevance: Information seeking is a chosen objective, not free. We must add it on purpose.

source: Millidge, Tschantz, Buckley (2021) Whence the expected free energy?
finding: Proposes the Free Energy of the Expected Future (FEEF), a KL between true-model and biased-model predictions. It keeps the information gain and adds an extra entropy term that pushes toward outcomes the model is unsure of.
numbers: FEEF = EFE with an extra veridical-model likelihood entropy term subtracted.
limits: Theoretical; the empirical comparison is in Tschantz (a16).
agent_relevance: Alternative objective if plain expected information gain under-explores.

source: Tschantz, Millidge, Seth, Buckley (2020) Reinforcement learning through active inference
finding: FEEF agent in model-based RL. On sparse-reward Mountain Car it reaches the goal in a single trial; reward-only and variance baselines mostly fail. On Cup Catch (easy to hit by chance) directed exploration gave no benefit. On Half Cheetah it beat SAC after 100 episodes. In reward-free Ant Maze it covers more maze than random.
numbers: Mountain Car: 25 episodes of up to 200 steps, 5 seeds, mean and SD plotted; optimal in a single trial. Cheetah: better than SAC at 100 episodes. Ant Maze: above random coverage (values only in figure).
quote: directed exploration afforded by our method provides little benefit
limits: Workshop paper, 5 seeds, curves not tables, 4 tasks. Benefit only where random actions do not find reward.
agent_relevance: Directed information seeking pays only when the answer is hard to stumble on. Test it against plain sampling at equal tokens (G7).

source: Friston, Da Costa, Hafner, Hesp, Parr (2021) Sophisticated inference
finding: Recursive expected-free-energy evaluation lets the agent consider what it will believe after acting, a tree search over beliefs. In the T-maze it makes epistemic choice more confident. Paradoxically the one-step agent underestimates the cue's epistemic value and stops cue-seeking a few trials earlier.
numbers: 32 trials, 2 moves each, planning horizon 2, path search cut when predictive probability < 1/16; preferences C = -2 and +2 (4 natural units between reward and punishment); reward arm paid 95%.
quote: there is a switch from explorative to exploitative behaviour
limits: Single task, deterministic MAP actions; comparison by trajectory, not statistics.
agent_relevance: Deeper look-ahead raises the worth of information and delays the switch. Planning depth is a real knob for when to stop exploring.

source: Friston et al. (2021) Sophisticated inference
finding: An agent using only Bayesian risk (no epistemic value) skips the arms and exposes itself to risk; epistemic value is what drives the cue visit.
limits: Toy comparison.
agent_relevance: Without an information term, a goal-only agent guesses.

source: Da Costa, Parr, Sajid, Veselic, Neacsu, Friston (2020) Active inference on discrete state-spaces: a synthesis
finding: Review pinning the terms: intrinsic value = epistemic affordance = expected information gain; about hidden states it is salience, about parameters it is novelty. It is mathematically the same as optimal Bayesian design and active learning, and underwrites artificial curiosity.
quote: curiosity resolves uncertainty about 'what would happen if I did that'
limits: Review of the discrete-state theory only; no new tests. Authors say the process theory needs Bayesian model comparison to test.
agent_relevance: Good vocabulary for our spec: salience (state info) versus novelty (parameter info).

source: Hafner, Ortega, Ba, Parr, Friston, Heess (2022) Action and perception as divergence minimization
finding: One KL objective unifies many exploration objectives. Latents over states give state information gain; over parameters give model learning (VIME, MAX, Plan2Explore); plain input entropy gives density exploration. Matching dynamics in the target removes the curiosity term.
numbers: Table 1 maps latents to objectives and agents.
limits: Unifying review, no new measurements.
agent_relevance: Information-gain exploration is one family with RL curiosity methods; borrow results from that literature.

source: Mirza, Adams, Friston, Parr (2018) Human visual exploration reduces uncertainty about the sensed world
finding: First model test on human eye-movement data. Models with the epistemic term explained scan-paths better for every subject. Models also needed non-epistemic reading-like heuristics. Subjects who relied less on heuristics were more accurate.
numbers: Pooled log evidence about 888 higher for the epistemic model than the preference-only model. Task: 20 practice trials, then 5 blocks of 100 trials (2 training, 3 test). Subject count not captured in my notes.
quote: substantial evidence for epistemic foraging in the visual exploration of even simple scenes
limits: Sample size not recorded here. Pooled evidence sums over subjects. Same lab that proposed the theory. Heuristic policies were added by hand.
agent_relevance: Human exploration is partly epistemic and partly habit. Expect both, and measure which wins.

source: Itti & Baldi (2009) Bayesian surprise attracts human attention
finding: Defines Bayesian surprise as KL between posterior and prior; reported to predict human gaze in video. Not opened. Opened sources say expected epistemic value equals expected Bayesian surprise.
limits: Known only through citation text.
agent_relevance: Prior art for the same quantity; check numbers before using.

source: Sun, Gomez, Schmidhuber (2011) Planning to be surprised: optimal Bayesian exploration in dynamic environments
finding: Earlier optimal-Bayesian-exploration work (information-gain curiosity) cited by all opened active-inference papers as ancestry. Not opened.
limits: Priority claims rest on citation text.
agent_relevance: Ancestor of the exploration bonus. Active inference adds the preference and ambiguity split.

source: Wilson, Geana, White, Ludvig, Cohen (2014) Humans use directed and random exploration to solve the explore-exploit dilemma
finding: Human behavioural evidence cited by Schwartenbeck 2019 that people use both an information bonus and noise (Horizon task). Not opened.
limits: Citation context only.
agent_relevance: If it holds, the agent needs directed probes and some randomness; G1 forbids scheduled doubt, so keep randomness in sampling only.

source: Gershman (2018) Deconstructing the human algorithms for exploration
finding: Cited by Schwartenbeck 2019 for random versus directed exploration (UCB-style bonus versus Thompson or softmax). Not opened.
limits: Citation context only.
agent_relevance: Competing account: a simple uncertainty bonus (UCB) can mimic epistemic value in bandits.

source: Kakade & Dayan (2002) Dopamine: generalization and bonuses
finding: Earlier novelty-bonus account cited by Schwartenbeck 2013. Not opened.
limits: Citation context only.
agent_relevance: Competing explanation: ad hoc bonus versus derived epistemic value.

source: Cross-read: Millidge 2021 versus Sajid 2021
finding: Two opened sources disagree on form. Millidge shows the epistemic term is not derived from free energy and offers a variant; Sajid keeps the original with ambiguity. So active inference does not give one curiosity formula.
limits: The variants differ in how much the agent seeks ambiguous outcomes.
agent_relevance: Do not claim the active inference answer; pick one formula and test it.

source: Cross-read: Sajid 2021 and Tschantz 2020
finding: Active inference gets exploration without a hand-tuned bonus, but both opened comparisons use small tasks. Neither tests it against UCB or Thompson-style bonuses, and neither uses language models.
limits: Gap in what I opened; LLM tests belong to the other angle.
agent_relevance: Prior: unproven as better than a simple bonus.

source: Cross-read: Hafner 2022 and Sajid 2021
finding: Pure input-entropy curiosity rewards rare inputs, so unlearnable randomness would attract it. Information gain about a latent is the guard, because it falls to zero when nothing can be learned.
numbers: Input entropy term described as encouraging rare inputs; information gain about a latent does not.
limits: The noisy-TV reading is mine; the opened text does not use that name.
agent_relevance: Probe choice must score learnable uncertainty, not just disagreement or surprise.
